title: Distance–speed–time reasoning
transcript: Speed tells you how far you travel in one unit of time. The three quantities are connected: distance equals speed times time. An average speed uses total distance and total elapsed time. It includes stops if the question includes those in the time.

In AMC practice, distance, speed and time often arrive in different units. Choose one time unit for your calculation first. A Rossmoyne style journey may have several stages. Work out each stage's distance or time before taking the average.
A cyclist covers twenty-four kilometres in three hours at a steady pace. Find the speed in kilometres per hour. What distance is covered in one hour?
Share twenty-four kilometres among three equal hours. Each hour covers eight kilometres. The speed is eight kilometres per hour. Multiplying back by the time recovers the full distance.
A rider moves at sixteen kilometres per hour for fifty minutes. How far do they travel? The rate already uses hours, so express the time as a fraction of an hour.

There are sixty minutes per hour. The travel time in hours is five over six. Multiply by the speed to get forty over three kilometres. If the time is below an hour, the distance is below the one-hour distance.

A rider travels thirty kilometres out at eighteen kilometres per hour, stops for eighteen minutes, and returns along the same route at fifteen kilometres per hour. What average speed covers the full trip including the stop?

Time equals distance divided by speed. The outward and return times are one hundred and one hundred and twenty minutes. Add the stop. The elapsed time is two hundred and thirty-eight minutes. The distance includes both legs, so it is sixty kilometres. Divide the total distance by that time in hours. The average is one thousand eight hundred over one hundred and nineteen kilometres per hour.

The two moving stages cover the same distance but take different amounts of time. A simple mean of the two speeds would give them equal time weights. The stop contributes time and zero distance. Including it in the average correctly reduces the overall rate.

Multiplying kilometres per hour by minutes uses inconsistent time units. Convert the time to hours first, or change the speed to kilometres per minute. Use one total distance and one total time. Do not average the speeds without checking how long you travelled at each.

Draw one row for each journey stage. Put speed, distance and time in matching units. For an average, check whether the time window includes stops. Add all the distances and the corresponding times first.
